note: DC-incident / outage glossary — terms and abbreviations used across the root-gated DC-Incidents dossier. Consumed by RZExplain (data-explain-scan / scanText).

blast-radius.d: The scope of everything affected when one component fails — how far a fault propagates into other systems, services and customers. Reducing blast radius (cells, regional isolation, bulkheads) is the central reliability lever after an incident.

cascading-failure.d: A failure that propagates: one component's outage overloads or breaks its dependents, which break theirs, amplifying a local fault into a systemic one. Retry storms and shared dependencies are common accelerants.

control-plane.d: The management/orchestration layer that provisions, configures and directs a system (e.g. launching instances, updating DNS, issuing tokens) — as opposed to the data plane that carries the actual traffic. Control-plane faults often cause wide outages even when stored data is intact.

data-plane.d: The layer that actually moves or serves traffic/data (packet forwarding, request serving), separate from the control plane that manages it. A data plane can keep running on last-known config while the control plane is down.

thermal-runaway.d: A self-accelerating failure in a battery (typically lithium-ion) where rising temperature drives exothermic reactions that raise temperature further, leading to venting, fire or explosion. A leading cause of data-center UPS-room fires.

lithium-ion-battery.d: High-energy-density rechargeable battery increasingly used for data-center UPS in place of lead-acid (smaller, longer life) — but with a thermal-runaway fire risk that has featured in several major DC fires (Kakao/SK C&C 2022, NIRS Daejeon 2025).

automatic-transfer-switch.d: Switch that automatically transfers the load between power sources (utility → generator) on loss of the primary. A stuck or mis-sequenced ATS can defeat backup power even when generators are healthy.

static-transfer-switch.d: Solid-state (thyristor) switch that transfers load between sources in milliseconds, e.g. the UPS output static switch. A failed output static switch took down Equinix LD8 (2020).

switchgear.d: The assembly of switches, breakers, busbars and protective relays that distributes and isolates electrical power in a facility. A switchgear failure severs the path between grid, generators and the load — as in the Delta Atlanta 2016 outage.

genset.d: Standby diesel/gas generator set that supplies the facility during extended utility loss, after the UPS bridges the start-up gap. 'Generators failed to start in time' is a classic power-outage root cause (Cloudflare/Flexential 2023).

de-energisation.d: Removing electrical power from equipment/a site. Slow or inaccessible de-energisation delays firefighting (water cannot be applied while current is present) — a key finding in the OVHcloud SBG2 fire.

free-cooling.d: Cooling that uses ambient air or water (economiser) instead of mechanical refrigeration, cutting energy. Some free-cooling airflow designs (open plenums, combustible materials) can accelerate fire spread, as investigators noted at OVHcloud SBG2.

chiller.d: The mechanical refrigeration plant that rejects data-center heat by cooling a water/glycol loop. Loss of chilled water forces temperatures up and can trigger protective server shutdowns within minutes (Azure Texas 2018).

failover.d: Automatic switch to a standby component/site when the primary fails. Failover that is untested, too slow, or itself depends on the failed system is a frequent reason a local fault becomes a long outage.

postmortem.d: Structured post-incident analysis documenting timeline, root cause and corrective actions. Blameless post-mortems are the reliability-engineering norm; an operator-published one is the gold-standard source for an incident.

correction-of-errors.d: Amazon's post-incident process/document that captures what happened, the root cause and the specific, tracked corrective actions to prevent recurrence. The 'COE' term is now used broadly for that discipline.

sequence-of-events.d: The precise, timestamped chronology of an incident from trigger through detection, mitigation and recovery — the backbone of any credible post-incident report.

rto-rpo.d: Recovery Time Objective (how fast service must be restored) and Recovery Point Objective (how much data loss is tolerable). The targets a DR/failover design must meet.

bgp.d: The internet's inter-network routing protocol that advertises which networks are reachable via which paths. A bad BGP withdrawal can make a company vanish from the internet — as when Meta withdrew the routes to its own DNS (2021).

dns.d: The system that resolves human names (example.com) to IP addresses. Because almost everything depends on DNS first, a DNS-layer fault (empty record, unreachable resolvers) causes broad, hard-to-diagnose outages (AWS DynamoDB 2025, Dyn 2016).

ddos.d: An attack that overwhelms a target with traffic from many sources (often a botnet) to exhaust its capacity. The Mirai IoT botnet's DDoS on Dyn (2016) disrupted much of the US internet.

iam.d: The service that authenticates identities and issues authorization tokens. Because nearly every request needs a token, an IAM/identity fault fails the whole platform even if compute and storage are healthy (Google 2020/2025).

retry-storm.d: A self-reinforcing overload where failing requests trigger aggressive client retries, multiplying load and sustaining the very congestion that caused the failures — effectively a self-inflicted DDoS (AWS Dec 2021).

race-condition.d: A latent bug where the outcome depends on the timing/interleaving of concurrent operations. A DNS-management race let one process overwrite another and delete the records in the AWS DynamoDB 2025 outage.

feature-file.d: A machine-generated configuration/data file pushed fleet-wide. When one doubled in size past a hard limit, it crashed Cloudflare's proxy globally (2025) — an example of unvalidated config as a blast-radius amplifier.

safe-deployment.d: Staged, ringed rollout with automated validation and fast rollback, intended to catch a bad change before it goes global. A latent defect in the rollback tooling turned an Azure AD update into a global outage (2020).

single-point-of-failure.d: A component whose failure alone takes down the whole system. Concentrating a globally-scoped control plane in one region (e.g. AWS us-east-1) creates systemic SPOFs.
